name: Neck fillers / skin boosters
lead: Neck fillers and skin boosters are clinician-administered injectables, most often hyaluronic acid (HA) gels, used to soften horizontal neck lines (sometimes called necklace lines) and improve the texture, hydration and firmness of neck skin. People use them to make the neck look smoother and more youthful so it matches the face, a common concern as the neck is often one of the first places age shows.

Two approaches are grouped under the name. Cross-linked HA fillers add structure and soften creases, while skin boosters are lighter HA or related products placed in the dermis to improve hydration, elasticity and overall skin quality rather than to add visible volume.[1][2] An expert consensus on non-animal stabilised HA skin boosters describes a typical plan of up to three initial sessions followed by a maintenance schedule, with continuing improvement in skin texture over months.[3]

Published neck-specific research found is mainly in the form of registered trials, including a 26-participant Restylane Refyne study of horizontal neck rhytides, alongside broader reviews of skin boosters and filler procedures.[4][5][6]

chain: HA gel placed in or just under the neck skin
Hydration and structure improve, creases soften
angle.text: Injected HA is used to soften horizontal neck lines and refresh the quality of neck skin so the neck looks smoother. People pursue it as a way to bring the neck in line with a youthful face.

infobox: Cross-linked HA fillers; HA skin boosters; biostimulators such as poly-L-lactic acid
Fillers are regulated as medical devices in the US and UK/EU

paras: Dermal fillers are injectable substances placed into the skin and underlying tissue, mostly to smooth wrinkles, restore volume and shape features; HA is among the most common because it occurs naturally in the body, is biodegradable, and most products are cross-linked to last longer.[7] The effect of fillers is temporary and is usually described as lasting around six months, depending on the product, the individual's skin and the injector.[7]

Skin boosters are a newer use of HA and related materials. A review describes a shift from using HA mainly to add volume towards delivering it to the dermis to improve hydration, elasticity and fine lines.[2] Reviews list other injectable materials used as boosters, including polynucleotides, PDLLA and exosome-based products.[8][9]

Neck treatment targets horizontal rhytides, the creases that run across the neck, and general crepiness or dullness of neck skin. A registered trial evaluated Restylane Refyne for correction of horizontal neck rhytides in 26 participants.[4] Another registered study tested a HA-based filler containing a vitamin, mineral and amino-acid complex, NCTF135HA, for anti-ageing performance and tolerance in 146 participants.[5]

Injections are given by clinicians, and an expert panel describing skin-booster practice notes that products placed in the dermis are intended to restore hydration and stimulate collagen, which in turn supports skin density.[3] Some practitioners combine injectables with energy devices; a registered trial examined Ultherapy after Sculptra treatment for skin laxity.[6]

Common reactions to fillers include bruising, redness, pain and itching; less often infection or allergic reaction occurs, and rare serious complications include vascular occlusion with tissue necrosis or, in the face, vision loss.[7] Regulators treat fillers as medical devices; in the US injection is by or under a licensed provider and in the UK and EU a larger number of products are marketed under CE marking.[7]

A 2025 narrative review of anti-ageing procedures discusses effectiveness and potential side effects across surgical and non-surgical options.[1] Individual pain and technique questions, such as intradermal versus subdermal placement of PDLLA boosters, have been examined in randomised split-injection research on the face.[10]

A completed registered trial (NCT04162496) evaluated Restylane Refyne for horizontal neck rhytides in 26 participants.[4] A completed registered study (NCT05609617) assessed NCTF135HA in 146 participants, and another (NCT01422538) studied Ultherapy after Sculptra for skin laxity in 30 participants.[5][6] The registry entries do not report results, so effect sizes are not given here.

Beyond the neck, an expert panel consensus on non-animal stabilised HA skin boosters recommends an initial series followed by maintenance and reports progressive skin-texture improvement for up to 12 months after repeat treatment at 4 to 6 month intervals.[3] A 2024 overview of injectable skin boosters reviews their types, mechanisms and clinical uses.[8]

timeline.event: A registered trial begins testing Ultherapy following Sculptra treatment for skin laxity.[6]
An expert panel publishes a consensus on non-animal stabilised HA as a skin quality booster.[3]
A registered trial of Restylane Refyne for horizontal neck rhytides begins.[4]

card.summary: Hyaluronic acid injections for neck lines; only registered trials found, no published results reviewed.
card.aka: Necklace line filler, neck skin booster

quick.overview:
Neck fillers and skin boosters are injectable treatments, typically hyaluronic acid, aimed at horizontal neck lines and skin quality.

The sources found are clinical-trial registrations, including a 26-person Restylane Refyne neck study, without published results to summarise.
quick.mechanism: A gel is injected into or beneath the skin by a clinician to add volume or hydration to creased areas.
quick.risks: Risks were not described in the sources reviewed. Fillers are administered by clinicians, and product regulation varies by country.
